transcript:
Header: 2025-12-29 11:00 PST | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya, Liam (Redwood); Sofia, Daniel, Priya, Evan (AtlasFin)

Summary: weekly POC sync - focused on sizing Dedicated pool and autoscale/burst behavior after pilot anomalies last week.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for joining, quick agenda—review last week's pilot numbers, discuss dedicated sizing and autoscale policy, and agree next steps. Sofia you had flagged a couple peak windows?
[00:18] Sofia (AtlasFin): yeah thanks. we saw two spikes last thursday and friday where p99 latency jumped and some requests timed out. overall p50's fine but p99s are a problem for checkout flows.
[00:33] Liam (SE): ok can you remind us of the traffic shape? is it a fan-out pattern or single big spike?
[00:40] Evan (AtlasFin): mostly fan-out; customer-facing endpoints cause many downstream LLM calls in parallel, plus batch jobs at 3am. peak concurrency was ~1.8k calls in a 30s window during the spike, average request size 220 tokens.
[01:00] Daniel (AtlasFin): and a bunch of those calls are stop-gap fallbacks to an internal rule engine, so latency is super sensitive.
[01:10] Liam: that helps. in the pilot we had a Dedicated pool with autoscale min 2 GPUs, max 10, scale step 1 GPU, cool-down 60s. the issue looks like the scaling reaction time + KV cache miss rate caused p99 to climb while new instances were warming.
[01:30] Priya (AtlasFin): can you explain the KV cache warming bit? we thought Dedicated would share caches across nodes?
[01:38] Liam: good question—KV cache is per GPU process; with autoscale adding new nodes you get cold starts until the cache is populated. Redwood has prefix/KV caching and proactive pre-warm hooks, but they need to be configured (cache prefetch + warmup policy).
[01:55] Maya: to add, there are also model-variant fallbacks—during capacity constraints we can route to a smaller quantized variant with lower latency and slightly different quality. that's part of the graceful degradation plan.
[02:10] Sofia: right, we want that as an option but only for non-sensitive endpoints. for fraud-check endpoints we can't degrade model quality.
[02:20] Priya: also this brings up security constraints: any pre-warm mechanism can't send sensitive data to external services, and KMS usage must be enforced for model keys. we need details on how Redwood handles KMS and audit logs.
[02:35] Maya: noted. we'll share the security whitepaper. quick question on cost tolerance—what's the acceptable delta if we increase base capacity to avoid p99 spikes?
[02:46] Sofia: we're willing to take ~15% higher infra cost during the pilot if p99 improves. long-term cadence we'd expect optimizations.
[02:55] Liam: ok that gives us a guardrail. so options: 1) increase min GPUs to reduce cold starts 2) aggressive pre-warm + shorter cooldowns 3) add burst capacity buffer on top of max (short-lived) 4) use model fallbacks for non-critical routes.
[03:12] Daniel: walk me through how burst capacity works — is it instant? how billed?
[03:18] Maya: burst is handled two ways: short-lived on-demand nodes in the Dedicated pool or routing to Redwood-hosted tiers as overflow. short-lived nodes spin up quickly (but still a few seconds) and are billed at higher rate for the burst window. overflow to hosted is typically slower to route but avoids capacity commits.
[03:37] Evan: any SLA on burst activation? we need worst-case numbers.
[03:41] Liam: worst-case spin-up 20-45s depending on GPU type and model warm time. with proactive pre-warm and cache prefetch we can get effective availability in under 15s for smaller models.
[03:55] Sofia: 20-45s is long for checkout. can we instead do sticky warm nodes reserved for peak hours?
[04:02] Maya: yes, you can schedule reserved capacity windows—set min capacity higher during expected windows, or use a rapidly scaling policy with pre-warm. that's why we recommended a two-tier autoscale policy in the spreadsheet.
[04:14] Liam: i'll explain the spreadsheet approach: baseline min 3 GPUs, reactive scale step 2 GPUs, cooldown 45s for normal; during predicted peak window set min 6 GPUs and allow burst to 12 for 10 minutes with pre-warm enabled. this reduces cold starts and p99.
[04:36] Daniel: can you quantify expected p99 improvement at those settings? like ballpark numbers.
[04:42] Liam: based on pilot traces, moving min to 6 and pre-warm reduces p99 from ~1.8s to ~650-800ms for the primary model, assuming cache hit rate improves to ~80%. tokens/sec throughput would go up ~2.2x under those settings.
[05:00] Sofia: cost impact? make sure we capture delta per hour.
[05:04] Maya: in the spreadsheet we'll show cost delta: baseline hourly +15% with min6 vs min3, and burst events add ephemeral cost. for Dedicated commits pricing applies for reserved nodes - burst on-demand is separate.
[05:16] Priya: about audit logs — we need immutable logs for each inference request, who called it, and key IDs used. is that available?
[05:23] Liam: yes, Redwood Console provides per-request tracing and audit logs, and we can integrate with your SIEM. KMS integration supports customer-managed keys (CMK) with HSM-backed stores and logs key usage in audit trail.
[05:36] Priya: sweet, please send the SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
[05:39] Maya: will do.
[05:41] Evan: back to the perf tests — can you run a perf run that mimics our concurrent fan-out of 1.8k calls with 220 token avg? we'd like to see p50/p95/p99 and GPU util over the run.
[05:51] Liam: yes we'll run that. plan to do two runs: one with current pilot policy and one with proposed two-tier policy and pre-warm. we'll capture token/sec, latencies, and quantized model behavior.
[06:03] Sofia: also can you include a run with fallback routing enabled so we can quantify quality vs latency tradeoffs?
[06:08] Liam: yes — fallback to a quantized 7B variant vs full 13B baseline. we'll measure differences in relevant eval prompts you provide.
[06:18] Maya: action item to exchange the eval prompt set — Sofia, can you share the 25 critical prompts used in checkout/fraud flows?
[06:24] Sofia: yes i'll upload to the shared drive today.
[06:28] Daniel: any changes needed on our side for VPC peering? last time we had some connectivity flaps.
[06:34] Liam: we noted the VPN MTU issue last week; for Dedicated we recommend direct VPC peering and a health-check path; we'll send network tuning suggestions.
[06:44] Priya: encryption at rest — ensure model artifacts and cached KV are encrypted with customer key.
[06:49] Liam: confirmed; Dedicated supports customer KMS and envelope encryption for caches and model artifacts.
[06:55] Sofia: curious about autoscale hysteresis — do you support step-down thresholds that are slower than step-up to avoid thrash?
[07:02] Liam: yes, you can configure asymmetric scale policies: rapid scale up (short cooldown) and slower scale down (longer cooldown and grace) to avoid flapping. we can propose default values in the spreadsheet.
[07:15] Evan: regarding monitoring—can we get token-level cost attribution by route? we need to map expensive endpoints to owners.
[07:23] Maya: Redwood Console supports per-route cost and latency breakdowns and assigns to API keys, so yes. we'll share screenshots.
[07:31] Sofia: last week you mentioned fallback routing to hosted tiers — any data residency concerns there? we can't send EU PII to non-EU regions.
[07:40] Maya: good call — overflow to hosted is region-aware; we can restrict overflow to same region or disable overflow for regulated routes. that'll be in config.
[07:52] Daniel: about the perf run infra—what GPU types will you use for the Dedicated test?
[07:57] Liam: we'll use the same GPU family as pilot, A800-class equivalent with 48GB, matching your pilot env. we'll note any kernel/compilation differences.
[08:05] Priya: one more on compliance — can you provide timeline for SOC2 attestation evidence and penetration test reports?
[08:12] Maya: we'll attach the SOC2 summary and pointer to attestation; penetration testing report is available on request via NDA.
[08:20] Sofia: ok great. any risks you foresee with the proposed two-tier policy?
[08:24] Liam: main residual risk is cache warm time during sudden, unpredicted spikes; we'll mitigate via pre-warm and sticky warm nodes. second is cost spike during repeated bursts — we'll model that in the spreadsheet and discuss commit vs on-demand tradeoffs.
[08:39] Maya: recapping next steps: Redwood will update sizing spreadsheet with two-tier autoscale and burst plan (Maya), SE will prepare perf tests (Liam), AtlasFin to share traces and eval prompts (Evan/Sofia), Security to confirm KMS checklist (Priya).
[08:55] Sofia: sounds good. can we get the updated spreadsheet by Friday?
[08:58] Maya: yes, target 2026-01-02.
[09:02] Daniel: let's schedule the perf run week of Jan 6th — i'll block time.
[09:06] Liam: we'll send proposed test windows after we get traces.
[09:10] Maya: anything else?
[09:12] Priya: nope, that's it from security.
[09:14] Sofia: thanks everyone.
[09:16] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up in email with docs and the spreadsheet.

End notes: transcript contains occasional ASR artifacts and speaker label noise. Referenced artifacts: dedicated-sizing-spreadsheet.xlsx (shared), security-whitepaper.pdf (to be shared), perf-test-plan.docx (to be delivered).
